detail.text: Every elementary fact about R(a) proved here is an upper bound or a finiteness statement: R(a) is finite and inside [2, a], one row per k, at most log2 a rows. None produces an a with exactly t rows for t >= 5, and none bounds #R(a) uniformly, so this route neither proves nor refutes the root. The affirmative side needs t simultaneous collisions C(n_i, k_i) = a, which no known family gives beyond t = 4 (a = 3003); the refuting side is Singmaster's conjecture, now the route variant-3969f1f7@1, w…

route.text: structural estimates on R(a) = rows holding a: row count = solution count (spec-12191c69), R(a) in [2, a] (spec-38faff03), #R(a) <= log2 a, rows with bounded k at most K (variant-3969f1f7--h1)

references.note: Lists the problem as open: 'There are no known examples for t ≥ 5'; Erdős and Singmaster believed the answer is no (an absolute bound on the number of solutions). Examples t=3: a=120; t=4: a=3003.
references.title: Erdős Problems #849 (T. Bloom, erdosproblems.com)

references.note: Proves N(a) = O(log a) for the number N(a) of representations a = C(n,k), and conjectures N(a) is bounded (Singmaster's conjecture). A bounded N would make the answer to Erdős 849 'no'.
references.title: D. Singmaster, How often does an integer occur as a binomial coefficient?, Amer. Math. Monthly 78(4) (1971) 385–386

references.note: N(a) = O(log a / log log a); Theorem 1: the average and normal order of N(a) is 2.
references.title: H. L. Abbott, P. Erdős, D. Hanson, On the number of times an integer occurs as a binomial coefficient, Amer. Math. Monthly 81(3) (1974) 256–261

references.note: Best unconditional bound: N(t) = O((log t)(log log log t)/(log log t)^3).
references.title: D. M. Kane, Improved bounds on the number of ways of expressing t as a binomial coefficient, Integers 7 (2007) #A53

references.note: For a large enough, at most two solutions with exp((log n)^(2/3+ε)) ≤ k ≤ n/2 (at most four in the whole interior region).
references.title: K. Matomäki, M. Radziwiłł, X. Shao, T. Tao, J. Teräväinen, Singmaster's conjecture in the interior of Pascal's triangle, Quart. J. Math. 73 (2022) 1137–1177 (arXiv:2106.03335)

references.note: Theorem 2.2: no collisions C(n,k)=C(m,l) beyond the known ones (3003 = C(78,2)=C(15,5)=C(14,6); 120, 210, 1540, 7140, 11628, 24310; and Lind's Fibonacci family) for n ≤ 10^6 and for C(n,k) ≤ 10^60. Conjecture 2.1 (de Weger 1997): there are no other collisions. If so, the multiplicities in rows are exactly 1, 2, 3, 4 and t ≥ 5 never occurs.
references.title: A. Blokhuis, A. E. Brouwer, B. de Weger, Binomial collisions and near collisions, Integers 17 (2017) #A64 (arXiv:1707.06893)

references.note: C(F_{2i+2}F_{2i+3}, F_{2i}F_{2i+3}) = C(F_{2i+2}F_{2i+3}−1, F_{2i}F_{2i+3}+1): infinitely many a occurring in at least 3 rows of the half triangle (at least 6 times in the triangle).
references.title: D. A. Lind, The quadratic field Q(√5) and a certain Diophantine equation, Fibonacci Quart. 6(3) (1968) 86–93; D. Singmaster, Repeated binomial coefficients and Fibonacci numbers, Fibonacci Quart. 13(4) (1975) 295–298

literature_proposed.summary: Open. Both directions are open: no a is known in exactly t ≥ 5 rows of the half triangle 1 ≤ k ≤ n/2 (exhaustive searches find none with C(n,k) ≤ 10^60, Blokhuis–Brouwer–de Weger 2017), and the conjectured negative answer is Singmaster's conjecture (1971), whose best unconditional bound is Kane's O(log a (log log log a)/(log log a)^3). Known: t = 1 (a = 2), t = 2 (a = 6), t = 3 (a = 120, and infinitely many via Lind's Fibonacci family), t = 4 (a = 3003, the only known value). Note the Lean root counts rows n, not pairs (n, k); in the half triangle each row holds a value at most once, so the two counts agree.

justification.text: Deliberate: k = 0 would count the trivial binomial C(n, 0) = 1, which the informal problem excludes.
Deliberate: t is the number of solutions and the problem asks about every t >= 1, inclusive.

import Mathlib

/-! Erdős problem 849: Is it true that, for every integer $t\geq1$, there is some integer $a$ such that ${n \choose k} = a$ with $1\leq k \le \frac{n}{2}$ has exactly $t$ solutions? — imported from google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/849.lean at c7f31d5fd3d2ca3d69979f2d213eb9b58fe956ae, Apache-2.0); the registry states a yes/no question as `answer(sorry) ↔ P`; this states P, its affirmative reading (F11-Q24). Drafted by gate/tools/wave.py (F14-T11) and read by the curator before import (R13). -/

open Nat

theorem Opn.erdos_849 :
    ∀ t ≥ 1, ∃ a : ℕ,
      {n : ℕ | ∃ k ≥ 1, 2 * k ≤ n ∧ choose n k = a}.ncard = t := by
  sorry
